question: Based on data from 2021, an estimated 49.6 % of household waste is recycled or composted, up 3.6 percentage points on 2017. These figures demonstrate an improvement in waste treatment, but overlook two crucial aspects: recycling is not yet automatic, as waste still has to be flared and buried; and the treatment of some kinds of waste is still sorely lacking.

At present, the simplest kinds of waste – such as paper, glass, metal and plastic – are sorted into separate bins. However, there are still problems with mixed household waste because it is often treated incorrectly and therefore loses its value. With the above in mind: 1.
How does the Commission intend to improve systems to better manage mixed household waste?
What steps has the Commission taken to encourage those involved at local and national level to better manage mixed household waste?
answer: To improve the management of municipal waste and reduce mixed residual waste from households, Member States have to achieve EU targets for preparing for re-use and recycling of municipal waste at 55%, 60% and 65% by 2025, 2030 and 2035, reduce landfilling of municipal waste to less than 10% by 2035; and set up systems for separate collection of at least paper, metal, plastic, glass and bio-waste and from 2025 hazardous waste from households and textile wast e (1).

Separate collection is key to ensure high-quality recycling and high capture rates. Waste that has been separately collected for recycling shall not be incinerated or landfilled (2). EU rules on products such as packaging and batteries aim to increase their recyclability and recycled content. The Commission has also proposed measures to reduce food waste and improve textile waste management. 2.

An Early warning report (3) recently assessed Member States’ likelihood of meeting the targets and recommended actions in country-specific documents, e.g. economic measures to reduce landfilling and incineration and improve waste prevention and recycling, such as landfill and incineration taxes, pay-as-you-throw and deposit and return scheme s (4).

The Commission has also issued guidance to Member States on separate collection of municipal waste, including best practices, and a report on developing an EU harmonised model for separate municipal waste collection (5); and supports Member States via technical assistance (6), exchange of best practices (7) and EU funds, e.g. the Recovery and Resilience Facility (8) and Cohesion Policy (9) funding (10).
The Commission has also set criteria for waste management activities under the EU Taxonomy (11), including the sorting of non-hazardous waste (12).
